paragraphs.heading: What an amino acid is
paragraphs.text: An amino acid is an organic compound that carries two working parts: an amino group and a carboxylic acid group. Nature holds more than 500 of them, but the 22 alpha-amino acids that go into proteins matter most by far. Those 22 are the only ones written into the genetic code. They are called proteinogenic, meaning protein-building, and ribosomes string them together into a vast range of peptides and proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Inside proteins, amino acid residues are the second-biggest ingredient of human muscle and other tissues, after water. They also do work outside proteins, for example in moving neurotransmitters around and in building other molecules. Scientists think amino acids played a key part in how life on Earth got started.

paragraphs.heading: The basic shape
paragraphs.text: Most alpha-amino acids share the general formula H₂NCHRCOOH. Here R stands for the side chain, the part that differs from one amino acid to the next. The α-carbon is the carbon atom sitting right beside the carboxyl group. In the protein-building amino acids it holds the amine group, the side chain and a hydrogen atom.

paragraphs.heading: Left and right hands
paragraphs.text: Apart from glycine, whose side chain is just another hydrogen atom, the α-carbon is stereogenic. Every chiral protein-building amino acid takes the L configuration, and these are described as left-handed, a name that refers to the arrangement around the α-carbon. A few right-handed D-amino acids turn up in nature, for example in bacterial envelopes, in some antibiotics, and as the nerve-signal modulator D-serine. On rare occasions D residues appear inside proteins, made by converting an L residue after the protein is built.

paragraphs.heading: Charged side chains
paragraphs.text: At neutral pH, five amino acids carry an electric charge. Aspartate and glutamate are the two with a negative charge, while arginine, lysine and histidine are positive. Histidine is a special case: only about 10% of it is protonated at neutral pH. Because it slips easily between its two forms, it often helps move protons around during enzyme reactions.

paragraphs.heading: How charge shapes proteins
paragraphs.text: Charged side chains often sit on a protein's surface, which helps the protein dissolve in water. Side chains with opposite charges can pair up in contacts called salt bridges that hold a protein's structure together, or link two proteins. Many proteins grip metal atoms, usually through charged side chains such as aspartate, glutamate and histidine. Other side chains, like those of serine, threonine, asparagine and glutamine, carry no charge but readily form hydrogen bonds with water and with other amino acids.

paragraphs.heading: Finding them
paragraphs.text: The first amino acid was found in 1806, when French chemists Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin and Pierre Jean Robiquet pulled a compound out of asparagus; it was later named asparagine. Glycine and leucine followed in 1820. The last of the 20 common ones, threonine, was found in 1935 by William Cumming Rose. In 1902 Emil Fischer and Franz Hofmeister each proposed that proteins are long chains of amino acids, with the amino group of one bonded to the carboxyl group of the next.
